question.text: In a two-stage DCF model, Terminal Value represents:

answer.text: The value of the company in its first year of operations
The present value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period, assuming stable growth
The liquidation value if the company shuts down immediately
The total dividend paid over the company's history

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook (pages 201-204), a two-stage DCF model separates high-growth-period cash flows from a terminal value that captures the perpetual stream beyond the explicit forecast period; the terminal value is then discounted to present value, often using the Gordon/perpetual-growth approach or an exit-multiple method. The Trap: Options A, C, and D are first-year, liquidation, and historical-dividend framings - terminal value is a forward-looking present value of post-forecast cash flows, not any of these. Note: When valuing with a two-stage DCF, always discount the terminal value back to today; small changes in the terminal growth or exit multiple assumptions can move the overall valuation significantly.
